Empirical Research Plan  

================================================================  
1. Identification Strategy  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Method: Multi-cutoff fuzzy Regression-Discontinuity Design (RDD) combined with 2-stage least squares (2SLS).

Rationale  
• The Ministry’s sequential assignment algorithm produces sharp admission score cut-offs at every oversubscribed secondary school.  
• Students who score just above a given school’s cut-off are admitted to that (more selective) school; those just below are diverted to a lower-choice, lower-achieving peer environment.  
• Because SEA scores are externally set, high-stakes, and graded centrally, students cannot precisely manipulate them, so observations on either side of each cut-off are quasi-random.  
• Assignment is not perfectly deterministic (20 % principal picks in Government-assisted schools and ties around the last seat), so the design is fuzzy; the cut-off indicator is a strong instrument for actually attending the more selective school / for mean peer quality.  
• Pooling 98 schools gives >90 separate score cut-offs, yielding high power and allowing us to trace heterogeneous (possibly non-linear) marginal effects across the school-quality distribution.  
• Gender interactions are estimated within the same local-RD framework.

================================================================  
2. Treatment and Control  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Treatment variable  
T_i = mean SEA score of all other students in student i’s assigned secondary school (a direct measure of peer quality).  
For interpretability we standardise T_i to mean 0, SD 1 within the cohort.

Instrument (running-variable discontinuity)  
Z_ij = 1{SEA score ≥ Cutoff_j} – indicator that student i’s score lies weakly above the admission threshold of her j-th ranked, oversubscribed choice.  
j indexes the school for which the student is marginal.

Control (counterfactual)  
Students scoring just below each cutoff (Z_ij=0). By construction they attend the next-best school on their choice list whose average peer score is lower.

Timing  
Running variable: centered SEA score, S_i – c_j.  
Cut-off: school-specific admission threshold c_j determined in May 2000.  
Outcomes are measured four and five years later in CSEC 2004/05.

================================================================  
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
A1. Continuity of potential outcomes at each cut-off: apart from school assignment, potential CSEC outcomes vary smoothly in SEA score.  
Plausibility: SEA is a single national exam; no curriculum or teacher changes occur exactly at the cut-off.

A2. No precise manipulation of the SEA score: density of scores is continuous at every c_j.  
Plausibility: external, machine-scored multiple-choice and essay exam; extremely hard to “game” within one or two marks.

A3. Local exogeneity of peer composition: being admitted changes mean peer achievement but not other unobservables locally.  
Plausibility: within a ±5-point SEA window, students are academically very similar; choice lists are fixed before score realisation.

A4. First-stage relevance: scoring above c_j strongly increases the probability of attending the higher-achieving school and raises peer quality.  
Documentable in data.

================================================================  
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigation  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Threat 1: 20 % discretionary seats in Government-assisted schools could blur the discontinuity.  
Fix: (i) treat design as fuzzy (2SLS), and (ii) show robustness to dropping the 20 % schools or to focusing on their non-discretionary 80 % of places (identifiable from detailed admission data).

Threat 2: Heterogeneous ordering of school choices could induce selection in the comparison set just below the cut-off (e.g., ambitious students might list only elite schools).  
Fix: restrict to students whose first-choice school is the margin school; include vector of choice-rank dummies; show covariate balance separately for each cutoff.

Threat 3: Sorting at the primary-school level might create bunching at certain scores (tutoring, cheating).  
Fix: McCrary density test at every cut-off and global pooled test; show balance in predetermined covariates (age, gender, religion, district). Fail-safe: trim any cut-offs with evidence of manipulation.

================================================================  
5. R Code Outline  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
```r
# 0. Packages -----------------------------------------------------
library(data.table)  # fast data
library(fixest)      # high-dim FE/IV
library(rdrobust)    # RD inference
library(ggplot2)

# 1. Load data ----------------------------------------------------
sea <- fread("SEA_2000.csv")      # SEA scores + choices + assignment
csec <- fread("CSEC_2004_2005.csv")

# 2. Merge & restrict to analytic cohort -------------------------
dt <- merge(sea, csec, by = c("lname","fname","dob","gender"), all.x = TRUE)

# 3. Construct outcomes ------------------------------------------
dt[, cert5 := (passes_total >= 5 & pass_english == 1 & pass_math == 1)]
dt[, tests_passed := passes_total]
dt[, math_grade_std := -1*(math_grade-6)]  # higher is better
# ...

# 4. Compute school-specific cut-offs -----------------------------
# For every oversubscribed school, find min SEA among admitted via rule
cut <- dt[, .(cutoff = min(SEA_score[assigned==1])), by = school_assigned]
dt <- merge(dt, cut, by.x = "school_of_margin", by.y = "school_assigned",
            all.x = TRUE)  # school_of_margin is marginal school for each kid

# 5. Running variable and instrument ------------------------------
dt[, score_centered := SEA_score - cutoff]
dt[, above_cut := (score_centered >= 0)]

# 6. Treatment: peer quality --------------------------------------
peer <- dt[, .(peer_mean = mean(SEA_score, na.rm = TRUE)),
           by = school_assigned]
dt <- merge(dt, peer, by = "school_assigned")
dt[, peer_z := scale(peer_mean)]  # standardised

# 7. Main fuzzy RD 2SLS (pooled across cut-offs) ------------------
bw <- 5  # ±5 SEA points (≈0.15 SD)
sample <- dt[abs(score_centered) <= bw]

fespec <- feols(cert5 ~ 1 | peer_z ~ above_cut,
                data = sample,
                cluster = ~school_of_margin)

etable(fespec)

# 8. Gender heterogeneity -----------------------------------------
fesex <- feols(cert5 ~ gender | peer_z ~ gender*above_cut,
               data = sample, cluster = ~school_of_margin)

# 9. Non-linear marginal effects ----------------------------------
# Interact instrument with decile of school selectivity
dt[, select_rank := ntile(peer_mean, 10)]
fesnl <- feols(cert5 ~ factor(select_rank) | peer_z ~ above_cut:factor(select_rank),
               data = sample, cluster = ~school_of_margin)

# 10. Robustness: bandwidth 3 & 7, covariate controls -------------
for(bw in c(3,7)){
  samp <- dt[abs(score_centered) <= bw]
  mod <- feols(cert5 ~ age + religion + district |
                 peer_z ~ above_cut, data = samp,
               cluster = ~school_of_margin)
  print(bw); print(summary(mod, stage = 2))
}

# 11. McCrary density test ----------------------------------------
rdensity(x = dt$score_centered, c = 0)$test
```

================================================================  
6. Expected Results  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
Economic intuition (peer-learning, motivation, teacher effort) predicts positive
effects. A one-SD increase in peer SEA achievement is anticipated to:

• Raise probability of earning the CSEC “certificate” by ≈ 4–6 percentage points (baseline ≈ 32 %).  
• Increase number of exams passed by ≈ 0.2–0.3 subjects.  
I expect slightly larger effects for females (evidence on cooperative learning) and diminishing marginal returns in the top decile of school quality.

================================================================  
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (RDD)  
----------------------------------------------------------------  
C1: Well-defined running variable & cut-off ………………… 1  
C2: No precise manipulation (density & covariate tests) … 1  
C3: Continuity of potential outcomes at cut-off …………… 0.8 (plausible but untestable)  
C4: Strong first stage / relevance ……………………………… 1  
C5: Local average treatment interpretation clearly stated … 1  

Total ≈ 4.8 / 5 — high internal validity conditional on standard RD diagnostics.

================================================================  
End of Plan
